cards.name: Aesthetic judgment and brand visual literacy
cards.includes: This bundle covers evaluating a body of creative work, such as print pieces or packaging graphics, against a brand standard and explaining what works, what does not, and why. It draws on major design principles and an understanding of how brand standards encode aesthetic decisions. Judgment is informed by accumulated visual references, not reduced to checklist compliance.
cards.excludes: Applying brand standards while creating or revising a deliverable belongs in brand-standards-application; developing a creative concept responsive to a brief belongs in conceptual-development. Building or operating a workflow review step for brand, legal, or print-quality checks belongs in quality-frameworks.
cards.distinctions: Unlike brand-standards-application, which applies standards to a deliverable, aesthetic-judgment evaluates a body of work and explains its visual strengths and weaknesses. Unlike conceptual-development, it judges creative work rather than generating a concept from a brief. Unlike quality-frameworks, it supplies aesthetic judgment rather than building or operating a repeatable quality and compliance review step.
positiveExamples: Critique a set of packaging designs against a brand standard, explaining which visual choices work and which do not.
Use design principles and accumulated visual references to explain why a group of print pieces feels consistent or inconsistent with a brand.
Identify aesthetic weaknesses in a body of creative work that passes explicit brand-rule checks, and explain the judgment.
negativeExamples: Revise a packaging layout to apply brand standards in an edge case (belongs in brand-standards-application)
Develop a campaign concept from a brief for execution across three media (belongs in conceptual-development)
Set up a recurring brand compliance review step for AI-assisted artwork (belongs in quality-frameworks)

cards.name: Agency
cards.includes: This bundle covers the habit of making and owning choices in one's work: choosing direction, scope or tools, setting goals, and following through without step-by-step direction. It is shown through behavior across assignments, such as graded choices in topic or approach and self-directed projects, not through instruction about agency.
cards.excludes: Planning and running a project's schedule and budget belongs in project-management. Going beyond requirements to investigate how things work belongs in curiosity.
cards.distinctions: Unlike curiosity, which is the drive to find out more, agency is taking ownership of decisions and outcomes. Unlike project-management, it is a personal habit of initiative rather than the skill of running a project plan.
positiveExamples: Choose and justify a project direction from an open brief, then carry it through without being told each step.
Set goals for a self-directed studio project and report progress against them.
Identify a better tool for a task and adopt it on one's own initiative.
negativeExamples: Build a project schedule with dependencies and re-baseline it after a change (belongs in project-management)
Research how a printing process works beyond what the assignment required (belongs in curiosity)
Revise a design repeatedly after critique until it works (belongs in resilience)

cards.name: AI literacy and responsible use
cards.includes: This bundle covers understanding in plain terms how generative AI produces output, why it can be fluent and wrong, and why the same request can give different results. It includes the rules for handling client and personal data in AI tools, why AI output must be checked before it is trusted, and why disclosure and content provenance matter for trust in brand and print work. In practice it shows up as explaining what a tool did and where it could be wrong, deciding what information may go into which tool, and disclosing AI-generated content as policy requires.
cards.excludes: Directing a tool through iterations to a finished output belongs in ai-tool-direction. Writing and operating a team's AI-use policy and review steps belongs in quality-frameworks. Rights and licensing in AI-generated assets belong in contracts-ip-licensing.
cards.distinctions: Unlike ai-tool-direction, which is skill in getting good output from a tool, ai-literacy is understanding what the tool is doing and following the rules for using it. Unlike quality-frameworks, which sets and runs the rules for a workflow, this bundle is the individual knowing and applying them. Unlike professional-responsibility, which is the habit of honest conduct, this bundle is the knowledge that conduct depends on.
positiveExamples: Explain to a client why an AI-drafted product description needs a fact check before it goes on a package.
Decide that confidential client artwork may not be uploaded to a public AI tool and choose an approved alternative.
Label AI-generated images in a deliverable according to the agency's disclosure policy.
negativeExamples: Iterate image prompts until the selected image meets the brand standard (belongs in ai-tool-direction)
Write a team's AI-use policy covering data, disclosure and sign-off (belongs in quality-frameworks)
Check whether a stock license permits use of an image in AI training (belongs in contracts-ip-licensing)

cards.name: AI strategy and change leadership
cards.includes: This bundle covers deciding where AI changes a creative, print or packaging organization and leading people through that change. It includes how falling production cost per version shifts pricing, offerings and roles; why adoption fails more often on people and process than on tools; and the parts of a change plan: roles, training, communication and measures. The practical work is developing an AI direction for a team, business unit or the organization's own operations and presenting it to decision makers.
cards.excludes: Benchmarking one AI tool to adopt, adjust or drop it belongs in ai-tool-evaluation. Writing and operating the AI-use policy and review steps belongs in quality-frameworks. Making the ROI case for a solution to win a client belongs in proposal-development, and managing an individual's performance belongs in team-coordination.
cards.distinctions: Unlike ai-tool-evaluation, which decides about one AI step from benchmark evidence, this bundle decides what AI means for the organization's offerings, pricing and roles. Unlike quality-frameworks, which writes and operates the rules, it sets the direction those rules serve. Unlike proposal-development, it plans the organization's own change rather than selling a solution to a client.
positiveExamples: Recommend how a print shop's service mix and pricing should respond as AI makes versioning cheap, with the roles that change.
Build a change plan for bringing AI into a creative team's work, with training, communication and measures of success.
Present an AI direction for an in-house brand studio to its leadership, including what changes for staff and clients.
negativeExamples: Benchmark an AI copy tool on the team's own work and recommend adopting or dropping it (belongs in ai-tool-evaluation)
Write the studio's AI-use policy on client data and disclosure (belongs in quality-frameworks)
Present a quantified ROI case for a client to buy an automated versioning service (belongs in proposal-development)

cards.name: AI tool direction and personal tool-building: prompt design, iteration, quality evaluation
cards.includes: This bundle covers directing generative AI tools for image, copy, and video work, from deciding which parts of a task to give AI and what a person must verify, through prompt design and iteration, to a final output that meets brand quality standards. It includes recognizing tool capabilities and failure modes, recognizing when not to use AI, and using human judgment to evaluate and improve results. It also covers scripting, assembling, or configuring a lightweight personal AI tool, prompt chain, or automation to speed one's own work, with documentation sufficient for reuse.
cards.excludes: Understanding how generative AI works and the rules for data and disclosure belong in ai-literacy. Organizational AI benchmarking and adoption recommendations belong in ai-tool-evaluation. Brand template or preset systems that produce compliant variations at scale for others to run belong in brand-system-templating. Engineering automated handoffs between creative, workflow, and AI systems belongs in systems-automation-integration.
cards.distinctions: Unlike ai-tool-evaluation, this bundle evaluates and improves outputs for the user's own work rather than benchmarking an organizational AI implementation for an adopt-or-drop decision. Unlike brand-system-templating, it builds reusable personal tools rather than maintained brand template systems documented for others to run. Unlike systems-automation-integration, its focus is directing AI and building lightweight personal aids, not engineering a handoff between two systems.
positiveExamples: Write and refine image-generation prompts, evaluating successive outputs until the selected image meets brand quality standards.
Split a brand copy task into parts for AI and parts for a person, direct the AI parts, and verify the facts a person must check.
Assemble a lightweight personal AI prompt chain for recurring creative work and document how to reuse it.
negativeExamples: Explain to a client how an AI tool can produce fluent but wrong copy (belongs in ai-literacy)
Build and maintain generative-AI presets that let a team produce on-brand campaign variations at scale (belongs in brand-system-templating)
Configure an API automation that handles a handoff between a creative system and an AI system (belongs in systems-automation-integration)

cards.name: AI implementation, benchmarking and evaluation
cards.includes: This bundle covers choosing and implementing an AI step in creative or production work, then benchmarking it on the organization's own work against the current process. It includes building a small test set and scoring rule, measuring output quality against references, error and failure-mode rates, cost per item, turnaround, and consistency across runs. It also covers recognizing drift as models change and writing an evidence-based recommendation to adopt, adjust, or drop the step that weighs quality, cost, risk, and staff workload.
cards.excludes: Prompt iteration and lightweight personal AI tool-building belong in ai-tool-direction; scripting or configuring handoffs between systems belongs in systems-automation-integration. Building or operating ongoing brand, legal/regulatory, or print-quality review steps belongs in quality-frameworks. Setting the organization's overall AI direction, roles and change plan belongs in ai-strategy-change-leadership.
cards.distinctions: Unlike ai-tool-direction, which focuses on directing and refining AI output for personal work, this bundle tests whether an implemented AI step warrants adoption in an organization's workflow. Unlike systems-automation-integration, it centers on benchmark evidence and the adoption decision rather than connecting systems and handling handoff failures. Unlike quality-frameworks, it evaluates the tool against the current process rather than establishing ongoing output review and accountability.
positiveExamples: Implement an AI-assisted artwork review step and compare its errors, turnaround, and cost per item with the current review process on a small set of actual jobs.
Build a reference set and scoring rule for AI-generated brand copy, then measure quality and consistency across repeated runs.
Rerun a workflow benchmark after a model change and recommend adopting, adjusting, or dropping the AI step based on quality, cost, risk, and staff workload.
negativeExamples: Iterate image-generation prompts until a brand deliverable meets the intended visual standard (belongs in ai-tool-direction)
Configure an API handoff that transfers artwork to an AI tool and handles failed transfers (belongs in systems-automation-integration)
Operate a recurring compliance review that catches errors in AI-assisted packaging artwork before release (belongs in quality-frameworks)

cards.name: Attention to detail
cards.includes: This bundle covers the habit of getting execution right as well as concept: correct file specifications, type, alignment, labels and spelling, and catching one's own errors before handoff. It is shown through work that is consistently clean across assignments and through rubrics that grade quality of execution, not only correctness.
cards.excludes: Operating a production inspection system with tolerances and accept/reject decisions belongs in quality-control. Checking packaging artwork against regulatory requirements belongs in packaging-artwork-compliance.
cards.distinctions: Unlike quality-control, which is a system for catching defects in production, attention to detail is a personal habit of careful execution. Unlike packaging-artwork-compliance, it is not tied to a defined checklist or regulatory requirement.
positiveExamples: Deliver print-ready files that meet every stated specification without correction.
Proof one's own layout and fix typographic and alignment errors before submitting.
Catch a mislabeled dimension in one's own dieline before it goes to a teammate.
negativeExamples: Set inspection points and tolerances for a production run (belongs in quality-control)
Check a package's required label text against regulations (belongs in packaging-artwork-compliance)
Calibrate a proofer to a color target (belongs in color-management)

cards.name: Brand positioning and messaging strategy
cards.includes: This bundle covers using brand architecture frameworks and positioning models to recommend what a brand should stand for, grounded in evidence about consumers and the market. In brand and packaging work, it includes weighing positioning alternatives and explaining the trade-offs that make a recommendation focused rather than trying to stand for everything. It addresses the strategic basis for brand messaging, not the production of finished copy or artwork.
cards.excludes: Designing and conducting consumer studies belongs in consumer-research, while producing a competitor analysis belongs in competitive-analysis. Translating an established positioning into coherent print, packaging, and digital executions belongs in cross-channel-translation.
cards.distinctions: consumer-research produces consumer insights, and competitive-analysis establishes the market context; brand-positioning uses that evidence to recommend what a brand should stand for and what it should leave out. cross-channel-translation carries an established positioning into print, packaging, and digital executions rather than choosing the positioning itself.
positiveExamples: Develop a packaging brand's positioning recommendation using consumer insights and market evidence.
Compare positioning alternatives and explain what the recommended position includes and deliberately leaves out.
Use a brand architecture framework and positioning model to support a brand positioning recommendation.
negativeExamples: Design and execute a consumer study, then synthesize its findings into an insight (belongs in consumer-research)
Produce a competitor analysis to inform a brand positioning recommendation (belongs in competitive-analysis)
Translate an approved brand positioning into coherent print, packaging, and digital executions (belongs in cross-channel-translation)

cards.name: Brand standards interpretation and application
cards.includes: This bundle covers reading a brand standards document, understanding its structure and scope, and applying its guidance to a creative deliverable such as a printed piece or package graphic. It includes interpreting guidance when the document does not directly address the situation and making choices consistent with its intent. The emphasis is on appropriate judgment in edge cases, not mechanically treating every guideline as a rule.
cards.excludes: Developing brand positioning belongs in brand-positioning, and building reusable templates or settings that generate compliant variations belongs in brand-system-templating. Managing packaging artwork versioning and checklist-based compliance belongs in packaging-artwork-compliance; building or operating a repeatable quality/compliance review step belongs in quality-frameworks.
cards.distinctions: Unlike aesthetic-judgment, which evaluates a body of work and explains its strengths and weaknesses, this bundle applies brand guidance while making a deliverable. Unlike brand-system-templating, it centers on judgment in a particular execution rather than encoding rules for automated variation. Unlike cross-channel-translation, it does not require coherent execution across print, packaging, and digital.
positiveExamples: Locate the relevant sections of a brand standards document and apply them to a print layout.
Interpret brand guidance for a package layout that is not illustrated in the standards document.
Resolve an ambiguous brand-guideline application in a creative deliverable using judgment consistent with the guidance's intent.
negativeExamples: Evaluate a collection of brand layouts and explain what works visually and what does not (belongs in aesthetic-judgment)
Build reusable layout templates that automatically produce on-brand variations (belongs in brand-system-templating)
Manage a packaging artwork version through a defined brand and regulatory compliance checklist (belongs in packaging-artwork-compliance)

cards.name: Brand system templating
cards.includes: This bundle covers translating brand and campaign rules into reusable templates, components, and platform settings that produce on-brand variations at scale for print, packaging, and other brand work. It includes building these systems in design tools, workflow platforms, or generative-AI platforms, with rules encoded precisely enough to guide automatic output. It also covers monitoring and maintaining the templates or settings as brand rules change and documenting how others can run the system.
cards.excludes: Interpreting brand standards for a single creative deliverable belongs in brand-standards-application. Configuring project intake, approval, and reporting steps belongs in workflow-architecture; connecting systems through scripts or APIs belongs in systems-automation-integration. Building a separate quality or compliance review step belongs in quality-frameworks.
cards.distinctions: Unlike brand-standards-application, which applies standards to an individual deliverable using judgment, this bundle encodes those standards into reusable systems that generate compliant variations. Unlike ai-tool-direction, which focuses on directing AI and building tools for personal use, it builds and documents brand-controlled templates or settings for others to run. Unlike workflow-architecture, which sequences intake, approvals, and reporting, it governs the brand rules built into output-generating templates and settings.
positiveExamples: Build reusable campaign layout templates with components and settings that encode brand rules for automatic variations.
Configure generative-AI presets to produce on-brand variations and document their use for other operators.
Monitor template-generated output and update the template system when brand rules change.
negativeExamples: Apply brand guidelines to a single campaign layout and resolve an unusual logo-placement case (belongs in brand-standards-application)
Iterate AI prompts to finish an image for one's own design project (belongs in ai-tool-direction)
Configure intake forms, proofing stages, and approval routing for campaign production (belongs in workflow-architecture)

cards.name: Client brief translation into creative direction
cards.includes: This bundle covers knowing the standard structure and expected contents of a creative brief and using that knowledge to interpret a real brand brief for print, packaging, or other brand work. It includes questioning ambiguities and assumptions rather than simply executing the brief's instructions. The resulting creative direction must respond substantively to the brief in a way its author recognizes.
cards.excludes: Discovery that produces a distinct client needs assessment belongs in client-needs-diagnosis; developing brand positioning from consumer and market evidence belongs in brand-positioning. Developing a creative concept and translating it across at least three executional media belongs in conceptual-development.
cards.distinctions: Unlike client-needs-diagnosis, which produces a needs assessment of the underlying business problem, brief-translation interrogates the brief to establish responsive creative direction. Unlike conceptual-development, it does not require developing a concept across at least three executional media. Unlike brand-positioning, it translates a supplied brand brief rather than developing a positioning recommendation from consumer and market evidence.
positiveExamples: Review a brand brief against the standard creative brief structure and identify missing or unclear information.
Question ambiguous instructions in a packaging brief to clarify their implications for creative direction.
Translate a real brand brief into creative direction that its author recognizes as substantively responsive.
negativeExamples: Conduct a discovery conversation and write an assessment of the client's underlying business needs (belongs in client-needs-diagnosis)
Develop a brief-responsive creative concept across print, packaging, and digital media (belongs in conceptual-development)
Recommend brand positioning based on consumer and market evidence (belongs in brand-positioning)

cards.name: Business and financial literacy
cards.includes: This bundle covers how a print, packaging, or marketing business makes money through revenue, cost of goods, gross margin, overhead, and pricing models. It includes explaining how a discount, rush job, or reprint changes profit and loss, and why higher volume does not necessarily mean higher profit. It covers reading a simple profit-and-loss or job-costing report and using numbers to explain whether a job or account is worth keeping.
cards.excludes: Preparing complex production estimates, managing delivery spend, and calculating equipment payback belong in cost-management. Negotiating price, scope, or terms belongs in negotiation-persuasion; writing and presenting a client proposal with a quantified ROI or total-cost-of-ownership case belongs in proposal-development.
cards.distinctions: Unlike cost-management, which develops production estimates, manages spend, and justifies equipment purchases, this bundle interprets revenue, costs, and profit to judge a job or account's financial value. Unlike negotiation-persuasion, it explains the financial effect of price or terms rather than conducting the negotiation. Unlike proposal-development, it evaluates profitability for the print, packaging, or marketing business rather than building a client-facing ROI case for a purchase.
positiveExamples: Read a print shop's simple profit-and-loss report and explain revenue, cost of goods, gross margin, and overhead.
Use job-costing figures to show how a discount or reprint changes a packaging job's profit.
Compare an account's revenue and costs to explain numerically why its high order volume does or does not make it worth keeping.
negativeExamples: Build a production cost estimate from packaging specifications, vendor capabilities, and run length (belongs in cost-management)
Negotiate a client's requested discount against a documented walk-away point (belongs in negotiation-persuasion)
Present a quantified ROI case showing why a proposed print solution pays for itself for the client (belongs in proposal-development)

cards.name: Campaign planning and effectiveness measurement
cards.includes: This bundle covers designing a measurement framework for a brand campaign involving print, packaging, or digital communications. It connects measures of success to business objectives rather than simply counting deliverables produced or distributed. It includes evaluating campaign results against those objectives to determine effectiveness.
cards.excludes: Client-facing post-project reporting to justify continued investment belongs in results-interpretation; general statistical interpretation belongs in quantitative-literacy. Planning and managing campaign production scope, schedules, budgets, and handoffs belongs in project-management.
cards.distinctions: Unlike results-interpretation, which centers on a client-facing post-project report, campaign-measurement defines how campaign success will be measured and evaluates results against objectives. Unlike quantitative-literacy, it applies data interpretation within a campaign-specific measurement framework rather than covering general statistical reasoning. Unlike project-management, it plans the measurement of campaign effectiveness, not the execution of creative and production work.
positiveExamples: Design a campaign measurement framework that links selected metrics to stated business objectives.
Distinguish measures of campaign effectiveness from counts of printed or digital deliverables.
Evaluate campaign results against the objectives specified in its measurement framework.
negativeExamples: Produce a post-project report that a client uses to justify continued investment (belongs in results-interpretation)
Interpret statistical significance and distinguish signal from noise in research data (belongs in quantitative-literacy)
Build and manage the schedule for producing and delivering campaign materials (belongs in project-management)

cards.name: Client needs diagnosis
cards.includes: This bundle covers critically reading print, packaging, or brand project briefs and asking discovery questions that surface needs the client has not stated. It addresses the gap between the requested deliverable and the underlying business problem. The work culminates in a written needs assessment that captures what discovery revealed, distinct from the original brief.
cards.excludes: Developing creative direction from a client brief belongs in brief-translation, and writing or presenting a solution proposal with an ROI case belongs in proposal-development. Managing client approvals, changes, and expectations through production belongs in project-oversight.
cards.distinctions: client-needs-diagnosis establishes what problem the client needs addressed; brief-translation turns a brief into responsive creative direction. proposal-development makes the business case for a proposed solution, while this bundle produces a written needs assessment rather than a proposal. project-oversight maintains client and team alignment during delivery, rather than diagnosing needs through discovery.
positiveExamples: Read a print project brief critically and identify assumptions to explore with the client.
Conduct a discovery conversation about a requested packaging redesign to uncover the underlying business problem.
Write a needs assessment that distinguishes the client's original request from needs surfaced during discovery.
negativeExamples: Translate a packaging brief into creative direction the client recognizes as responsive (belongs in brief-translation)
Write a print solution proposal with a quantified cost/benefit case (belongs in proposal-development)
Coordinate client proof approvals and communicate production schedule changes (belongs in project-oversight)

cards.name: Collaboration and teamwork
cards.includes: This bundle covers working well with others on shared work: dividing tasks, keeping commitments, integrating others' contributions and working through disagreement so the group's result is better than any one member's. It is shown through team projects where individual contribution and the group's working process are assessed.
cards.excludes: Managing staff roles, performance and hiring belongs in team-coordination. Running the project plan belongs in project-management.
cards.distinctions: Unlike team-coordination, which is the manager's responsibility for a team, collaboration is being a good member of one. Unlike project-management, it is how a person works with others, not how the project's schedule and budget are run.
positiveExamples: Divide a team packaging project fairly and deliver one's part on time.
Integrate a teammate's work into a shared design so the result is consistent.
Work through a disagreement about direction and reach a decision the team carries out.
negativeExamples: Conduct a performance review for a production team member (belongs in team-coordination)
Build and re-baseline the team project's schedule (belongs in project-management)
Present the team's project to the class (belongs in spoken-communication)

cards.name: Color management
cards.includes: This bundle covers setting up a print or packaging process to reproduce color to a defined target: device calibration (including G7 gray-balance calibration), ICC profiling for a device and substrate, and the color targets set by standards such as ISO 12647. It addresses why color drifts across devices and substrates and treats color accuracy as measurable rather than a visual preference. It includes setting up or auditing the color setup for a real job and proving with measurements, such as Delta E against a reference, that the setup reproduces the target.
cards.excludes: Monitoring a running job against tolerances, statistical process control, and accept/reject decisions belong in quality-control, which watches color alongside every other defect. Selecting substrates or finishing based on production suitability belongs in domain-knowledge, and interpreting brand guidelines for a creative deliverable belongs in brand-standards-application.
cards.distinctions: Unlike quality-control, which runs the system that catches any defect while a job is produced and decides whether it ships, color-management sets up color reproduction before the run: calibration, profiles, and color targets. Unlike domain-knowledge, it actively sets up color reproduction rather than judging general process, material, and equipment suitability. Unlike brand-standards-application, it proves reproduced color against a measured target rather than interpreting brand rules for a creative deliverable.
positiveExamples: Calibrate a press to G7 gray balance and verify the result with measurements.
Build ICC profiles for a packaging job's devices and substrate, then measure a proof against the reference to confirm the color target is met.
Audit a print job's color setup to find why output drifts from its target and correct the calibration or profile.
negativeExamples: Monitor a running job's color and registration against tolerances and decide whether it ships (belongs in quality-control)
Choose a packaging substrate and finishing process based on production constraints (belongs in domain-knowledge)
Interpret brand guidelines when applying a color palette to a creative deliverable (belongs in brand-standards-application)

cards.name: Competitive and market analysis
cards.includes: This bundle covers using competitive analysis frameworks and sourcing competitor data to examine the market context for a brand. In graphic communications work, that can include comparing competitors' messaging and brand presentation in print, packaging, and digital materials. It covers producing an analysis that explains how competitive context limits or opens positioning options and informs a positioning recommendation.
cards.excludes: Developing the overall brand positioning and messaging recommendation belongs in brand-positioning; designing and executing consumer research belongs in consumer-research. Evaluating creative work against a brand standard belongs in aesthetic-judgment.
cards.distinctions: Unlike brand-positioning, this bundle produces the competitive evidence that informs a positioning recommendation rather than developing the overall positioning strategy. Unlike consumer-research, it examines competitors and competitive context rather than designing a consumer study. Unlike aesthetic-judgment, it compares brand expressions for their competitive implications rather than judging creative work against a brand standard.
positiveExamples: Identify sources of competitor data for a packaging brand's competitive analysis.
Use a competitive analysis framework to compare competing brands' messaging and packaging presentation.
Produce a competitive analysis explaining which positioning options the competitor landscape supports or constrains.
negativeExamples: Develop a brand positioning recommendation using consumer and market evidence (belongs in brand-positioning)
Design and conduct a consumer study, then synthesize a strategic insight (belongs in consumer-research)
Evaluate packaging designs against the client's brand standard (belongs in aesthetic-judgment)

cards.name: Conceptual development and creative ideation across disciplines
cards.includes: This bundle covers using ideation methods to develop a creative concept that responds to a graphic communications brief. It treats the brief's constraints as the discipline that guides creative choices, rather than treating ideation as unrestricted idea generation. It includes translating the concept across at least three executional media, such as print, image, and video, while retaining the central idea.
cards.excludes: Producing finished creative deliverables across media belongs in cross-medium-production; translating brand positioning coherently across print, packaging, and digital belongs in cross-channel-translation. Evaluating creative work against brand standards belongs in aesthetic-judgment.
cards.distinctions: Unlike brief-translation, which emphasizes interrogating a brief and establishing responsive creative direction, conceptual-development emphasizes generating a creative concept under the brief's constraints and translating it across at least three executional media. Unlike cross-channel-translation, its starting point is a brief-driven creative concept rather than a single brand positioning. Unlike cross-medium-production, it focuses on developing and translating the idea, not producing finished work across media.
positiveExamples: Use ideation methods to generate creative concepts guided by a packaging campaign brief's constraints.
Develop one brief-responsive concept and show how it translates into print, image, and video.
Refine a concept's expressions across three media so each remains responsive to the brief.
negativeExamples: Produce finished copy, images, and video for a single brand project (belongs in cross-medium-production)
Translate a brand positioning into coherent print, packaging, and digital executions (belongs in cross-channel-translation)
Evaluate campaign designs against a brand standard and explain what works and why (belongs in aesthetic-judgment)

cards.name: Consumer research and insight synthesis
cards.includes: This bundle covers selecting appropriate qualitative or quantitative methods and designing and carrying out consumer research for brand, print, or packaging questions. It includes interpreting findings together to develop a strategic insight about consumers, rather than merely listing responses or reporting results.
cards.excludes: Competitor research and analysis belong in competitive-analysis, and developing a brand positioning recommendation belongs in brand-positioning. General statistical interpretation without designing and executing a consumer study belongs in quantitative-literacy.
cards.distinctions: Unlike quantitative-literacy, which emphasizes critically interpreting research data, consumer-research covers choosing methods, designing and executing a consumer study, and synthesizing its findings. Unlike competitive-analysis, it investigates consumers rather than competitor context. Unlike brand-positioning, it produces a strategic consumer insight rather than a recommendation about what the brand should stand for.
positiveExamples: Choose a qualitative or quantitative research method suited to a question about consumers' responses to packaging.
Design and conduct a consumer study exploring how people interpret a brand's printed messaging.
Synthesize consumer study findings into a strategic insight that explains the meaning behind observed responses.
negativeExamples: Compare competing brands' packaging and messaging to inform positioning (belongs in competitive-analysis)
Develop a brand positioning recommendation from consumer and market evidence (belongs in brand-positioning)
Assess whether a reported statistical difference is practically meaningful (belongs in quantitative-literacy)

cards.name: Contracts, IP and licensing
cards.includes: This bundle covers basic contract terms for print, packaging, and brand jobs, including scope, payment, liability, and change orders. It covers copyright, trademarks, font and image licensing, and rights in AI-generated content as they apply to a job's assets and intended use. It includes reviewing assets and agreements, identifying who carries risk in the client–vendor chain, and resolving licensing and contract risks before release, when late discoveries would be most costly.
cards.excludes: Asset-library metadata, taxonomy, and rights-tracking structures belong in digital-asset-management, not here. Conducting negotiations over price, scope, or terms belongs in negotiation-persuasion. Building a workflow-wide quality or compliance review step belongs in quality-frameworks.
cards.distinctions: Unlike digital-asset-management, which organizes assets and tracks rights for reuse, this bundle evaluates whether a job's intended use is permitted and resolves rights risks. Unlike negotiation-persuasion, which focuses on reaching agreement over price, scope, or terms, it focuses on understanding contract terms and addressing their risks. Unlike quality-frameworks, which builds or operates repeatable compliance review steps, it supplies the contract and IP judgment needed to review a specific job.
positiveExamples: Review font and image licenses against a packaging job's intended use and resolve permission gaps before release.
Review scope, payment, liability, and change-order terms in a client–vendor agreement and resolve identified risks.
Check copyright, trademark, and AI-generated-content rights in brand artwork before release.
negativeExamples: Configure rights metadata and search categories in an asset library (belongs in digital-asset-management)
Negotiate a client's price and scope against a defined walk-away point (belongs in negotiation-persuasion)
Build a repeatable compliance review step for AI-assisted production output (belongs in quality-frameworks)

cards.name: Cost estimation, budget management, and equipment justification
cards.includes: This bundle covers the cost structures of major print and packaging processes and the preparation of defensible estimates for complex production projects, reconciling specifications, vendor capabilities, and run-length economics. It includes managing project spend through delivery. It also covers capital-equipment justification based on purchase cost, throughput or quality gain, and payback over multiple years, distinct from estimating a single job or judging its margin.
cards.excludes: Full-project scheduling, scope control, and close-out belong in project-management; selecting, briefing, and managing vendor relationships belong in vendor-management. Reading profit-and-loss reports to assess job or account profitability belongs in business-financial-literacy, while writing and presenting a client proposal with an ROI case belongs in proposal-development.
cards.distinctions: Unlike business-financial-literacy, which interprets profitability and financial reports, cost-management builds production estimates and controls project spend. Unlike project-management, which runs the full project life cycle, it focuses on the cost basis and spending through delivery. Unlike proposal-development, which presents a solution's business case to win client commitment, it justifies production equipment using purchase cost, throughput or quality gain, and multi-year payback.
positiveExamples: Estimate a complex packaging project's cost by reconciling specifications, vendor capabilities, and run-length economics.
Track production spending against the estimate and manage the budget through delivery.
Build an equipment-purchase case showing purchase cost, expected throughput or quality gain, and multi-year payback.
negativeExamples: Build a production schedule with dependencies and track scope changes through close-out (belongs in project-management)
Read a job-costing report to explain whether an account is worth keeping (belongs in business-financial-literacy)
Write and present a client proposal with a quantified ROI case to secure commitment (belongs in proposal-development)

cards.name: Cross-channel brand translation (print, packaging, digital)
cards.includes: This bundle covers translating a single brand positioning into coherent print, packaging, and digital executions. It includes recognizing how brand standards manifest differently in physical and digital channels and adapting their expression to each. The focus is deliberate translation that preserves a consistent brand identity without simply duplicating the same execution everywhere.
cards.excludes: Developing the brand positioning itself belongs in brand-positioning; building reusable templates or settings that generate on-brand variations at scale belongs in brand-system-templating. Calibrating devices, profiling, and setting up measurable color reproduction belong in color-management.
cards.distinctions: Unlike brand-standards-application, which focuses on interpreting standards for a creative deliverable, this bundle focuses on coherent brand execution across physical and digital channels. Unlike conceptual-development, it translates an established brand positioning rather than developing a creative concept from a brief. Unlike cross-medium-production, its defining concern is cross-channel brand coherence, not the breadth of finished media produced.
positiveExamples: Translate one brand positioning into coordinated brochure, package, and website executions.
Adapt the expression of brand typography and imagery across print, packaging, and digital while preserving a coherent identity.
Revise channel-specific executions that duplicate one layout so each expresses the same brand appropriately for its channel.
negativeExamples: Develop a brand positioning recommendation based on consumer and market evidence (belongs in brand-positioning)
Build reusable brand templates that produce compliant variations at scale (belongs in brand-system-templating)
Calibrate and profile print devices to meet a defined brand color standard (belongs in color-management)

cards.name: Cross-medium creative production (copy, design, image, video, print)
cards.includes: This bundle covers producing finished work across at least three creative media for a single brand project, drawing on copy, design, image, video, and print production. It includes knowing and working within the production constraints and standards of the media used. The emphasis is on generalist fluency across disciplines, not specialization in any one medium.
cards.excludes: Developing the underlying creative concept belongs in conceptual-development; translating brand positioning coherently across print, packaging, and digital belongs in cross-channel-translation. Interpreting brand guidelines and resolving their edge cases belongs in brand-standards-application.
cards.distinctions: Unlike conceptual-development, which develops a concept that translates across media, this bundle carries execution through to finished work in at least three creative media. Unlike cross-channel-translation, which emphasizes coherent brand expression across print, packaging, and digital channels, this bundle emphasizes production fluency across creative disciplines such as copy, design, image, and video. Brand-standards-application focuses on interpreting brand rules for a deliverable rather than producing a multi-media body of finished work.
positiveExamples: Produce finished copy, images, and video for a single brand project.
Complete print, image, and video deliverables while meeting each medium's production constraints and standards.
Explain how production requirements differ across copy, image, video, and print work.
negativeExamples: Develop a creative concept and show how it could extend into three media (belongs in conceptual-development)
Translate brand positioning into coherent print, packaging, and digital expressions (belongs in cross-channel-translation)
Resolve an ambiguous brand-guideline rule for a layout (belongs in brand-standards-application)

cards.name: Curiosity
cards.includes: This bundle covers the habit of going beyond stated requirements to find out how and why things work: seeking sources, techniques or questions an assignment did not require. It is shown where courses reward going beyond the criteria, such as open-inquiry components or graded exploration.
cards.excludes: Taking ownership of choices and follow-through belongs in agency. Designing and running consumer studies belongs in consumer-research.
cards.distinctions: Unlike agency, which is ownership of decisions, curiosity is the drive to understand more. Unlike consumer-research, it is a personal habit of inquiry, not a research method applied for a client.
positiveExamples: Investigate why an ink behaves differently on two substrates beyond what the lab asked.
Try a technique not taught in class and report what it shows.
Bring an outside source into a project that changes the team's approach.
negativeExamples: Choose and own a project direction from an open brief (belongs in agency)
Design a survey to understand target consumers' packaging preferences (belongs in consumer-research)
Revise work repeatedly after critique (belongs in resilience)

cards.name: Customer relationship and service
cards.includes: This bundle covers customer service standards, problem escalation, and long-term account retention in print, packaging, and brand work. It includes managing a client through a missed delivery date or quality complaint to a recorded resolution, and maintaining a relationship record another staff member can pick up. It addresses how handling a mistake well can build trust and why retaining a client costs less than acquiring a new one.
cards.excludes: Routine project approvals, handoffs, and expectation management belong in project-oversight. Negotiating price, scope, or terms belongs in negotiation-persuasion, and setting up production checks to prevent quality failures belongs in quality-control.
cards.distinctions: Unlike project-oversight, which keeps clients and production teams aligned through approvals and changes, this bundle centers on service recovery and continuity of the client relationship. Unlike negotiation-persuasion, it focuses on handling client problems rather than bargaining over price, scope, or terms. Unlike vendor-management, it maintains the customer relationship rather than the relationship with a production supplier.
positiveExamples: Manage a client's missed-delivery complaint through escalation and document the resolution.
Handle a packaging quality complaint according to service standards while maintaining client trust.
Update the client relationship record with the problem, response, and resolution so another staff member can continue service.
negativeExamples: Coordinate client sign-offs on proofs and production changes (belongs in project-oversight)
Negotiate a revised job price against a defined walk-away point (belongs in negotiation-persuasion)
Set up inspection checks to prevent recurring print defects (belongs in quality-control)

cards.name: Digital asset management
cards.includes: This bundle covers organizing a real library of brand, print, or packaging assets in a DAM or DAM-like system using metadata, taxonomy, and rights information. It includes setting up or maintaining that structure and demonstrating that users can find assets and reuse them correctly. It addresses how weak metadata and taxonomy compound as a library grows, and treats rights tracking as a compliance requirement.
cards.excludes: Reviewing agreements and resolving licensing risks belongs in contracts-ip-licensing; recording rights so library assets can be reused correctly belongs here. Managing packaging artwork versions and checking labeling or print compliance belongs in packaging-artwork-compliance. Configuring project intake and approval steps belongs in workflow-architecture.
cards.distinctions: Unlike contracts-ip-licensing, this bundle tracks rights within an asset library rather than resolving a job's licensing or contract risks. Unlike packaging-artwork-compliance, it organizes assets for discovery and correct reuse rather than managing packaging artwork through versioning and compliance checks. Unlike workflow-architecture, it configures the library's metadata and taxonomy rather than sequencing intake, approvals, proofing, and reporting.
positiveExamples: Set up metadata fields and taxonomy terms for a real library of brand images and packaging graphics.
Maintain asset rights metadata so users can identify which images are permitted for a proposed reuse.
Test searches in a DAM to demonstrate that assets can be found and reused correctly, and correct metadata gaps exposed by the test.
negativeExamples: Review an image license and resolve a usage restriction before a print job is released (belongs in contracts-ip-licensing)
Manage packaging artwork revisions and check required label text before approval (belongs in packaging-artwork-compliance)
Configure a platform's creative intake, proofing, and approval sequence (belongs in workflow-architecture)

cards.name: Production domain knowledge: processes, substrates, materials and equipment
cards.includes: This bundle covers knowledge of print, packaging, and brand production processes, substrates, inks, finishing, equipment, and technology, including their capabilities and limitations. It applies that knowledge to selecting substrates and finishing, accurately briefing a production team or sales engineer, and judging whether a design or specification is producible and fit for purpose. It also covers explaining, with specific production reasons, why a workflow, template, or AI output would succeed or fail and how production constraints shape creative and commercial possibilities.
cards.excludes: Color profiling and calibration belong in color-management. Designing or re-engineering production workflows belongs in workflow-design, and setting up and operating production defect checks and process control belongs in quality-control. Building or configuring an automation between systems belongs in systems-automation-integration, rather than here.
cards.distinctions: Unlike workflow-design, this bundle supplies the production knowledge used to judge whether a workflow will work rather than designing or re-engineering the production process. Unlike quality-control, it judges feasibility and fitness for purpose from material, process, and equipment constraints rather than setting up a conformance system. Unlike cost-management, it explains what production choices make possible rather than calculating job costs or equipment payback.
positiveExamples: Specify a substrate and finishing combination that suits a packaging job and the available equipment.
Brief a production team on the material and process limitations affecting a proposed print design.
Explain why an AI-generated packaging concept cannot be produced as shown, citing specific substrate and finishing constraints.
negativeExamples: Calibrate a print device and verify that a job meets a defined color standard (belongs in color-management)
Re-engineer a production step and validate its throughput and quality gains (belongs in workflow-design)
Build a purchase-cost and payback case for finishing equipment (belongs in cost-management)

cards.name: Negotiation and persuasion
cards.includes: This bundle covers preparing and conducting real or simulated negotiations over price, scope, or terms for print, packaging, or brand work. It includes distinguishing underlying interests from stated positions, establishing walk-away points, and using price, terms, and scope as negotiating levers. It emphasizes protecting both margin and the relationship, and documenting the outcome against the walk-away point.
cards.excludes: Writing and presenting a proposal with a quantified ROI case belongs in proposal-development. Reviewing agreements and assets for contract or licensing risks belongs in contracts-ip-licensing. Managing client service problems and maintaining relationship records belongs in customer-relationship-management.
cards.distinctions: Unlike proposal-development, which builds and presents the business case for a solution, this bundle handles bargaining over price, scope, or terms against a walk-away point. Unlike contracts-ip-licensing, it focuses on reaching an acceptable deal rather than identifying and resolving contract or rights risks. Unlike customer-relationship-management, it protects the relationship during negotiation rather than managing service problems and ongoing account records.
positiveExamples: Prepare for a print-price negotiation by identifying interests, stated positions, and a walk-away point.
Conduct a simulated packaging negotiation using trade-offs among price, scope, and payment terms to protect margin and the relationship.
Document agreed brand-project scope and terms and compare the outcome with the established walk-away point.
negativeExamples: Write and present a packaging proposal with a quantified cost-benefit case (belongs in proposal-development)
Review a print job agreement for liability and image licensing risks (belongs in contracts-ip-licensing)
Resolve a client's quality complaint and update the account's relationship record (belongs in customer-relationship-management)

cards.name: Packaging artwork workflow and compliance
cards.includes: This bundle covers the packaging artwork production pipeline, including artwork management, version control, and the regulatory and print-quality requirements governing packaging graphics. It includes managing a packaging artwork file through revisions and a regulatory, brand, or print-quality compliance check using a defined checklist or an AI-assisted review tool. It also covers recognizing why labeling errors and missed requirements are costly and how versioning discipline prevents those failures.
cards.excludes: Asset-library taxonomy and metadata management belong in digital-asset-management; workflow platform configuration and approval sequencing belong in workflow-architecture. Setting up a production quality control system belongs in quality-control, rather than checking a packaging artwork file against defined requirements.
cards.distinctions: Unlike digital-asset-management, this bundle centers on version control and compliance of a packaging artwork file, not metadata and reuse across an asset library. Unlike quality-frameworks, it specifically ties review to the packaging artwork pipeline and versioning discipline. Unlike workflow-architecture, it manages artwork within a defined workflow rather than designing or configuring the workflow itself.
positiveExamples: Track revisions to a packaging artwork file and check the current version against a labeling compliance checklist.
Manage a packaging artwork revision through a defined brand or print-quality check.
Use an AI-assisted review tool to check the current packaging artwork version for missed regulatory requirements.
negativeExamples: Build a metadata taxonomy so packaging assets can be found and reused across a library (belongs in digital-asset-management)
Configure a platform's intake, approval, proofing, and reporting sequence (belongs in workflow-architecture)
Set up a production quality control system using industry standards and conformance measurements (belongs in quality-control)

cards.name: Problem solving in the discipline
cards.includes: This bundle covers solving unfamiliar production, design and business problems in graphic communications by bringing organized domain knowledge to bear: diagnosing what is wrong, attempting a solution, learning from failed attempts and revising, across varied conditions. It is a program-level outcome, developed through repeated cycles of productive failure and structured reflection at increasing depth, and is not scored course by course.
cards.excludes: Following a known procedure correctly belongs in the technical bundle for that procedure. Persisting through setbacks as a personal habit belongs in resilience, and going beyond requirements to find out how things work belongs in curiosity.
cards.distinctions: Unlike the technical bundles, which each describe one area of skill, problem solving is what those skills become when students deploy them on unfamiliar problems. Unlike resilience and curiosity, which are habits, it is the capability those habits help build. Unlike a generic reasoning skill, it does not transfer apart from domain knowledge.
positiveExamples: Diagnose why a packaging run shows an unfamiliar defect, test likely causes, and fix it.
Work out a production approach for a job no standard workflow fits, learning from a failed first attempt.
Reframe a client's problem after an initial solution fails and develop one that works.
negativeExamples: Calibrate a press to a known color target by following the standard procedure (belongs in color-management)
Keep revising a design after several rounds of critique (belongs in resilience)
Research how a printing process works beyond what the lab required (belongs in curiosity)

cards.name: Professional responsibility and ethics
cards.includes: This bundle covers acting with professional integrity: representing one's own and others' work honestly (including AI's part), respecting intellectual property and confidentiality, meeting commitments, and owning mistakes. It is shown through conduct across courses and projects, such as attribution, handling of client materials and honesty about errors.
cards.excludes: Knowing contract terms and licensing rules belongs in contracts-ip-licensing. Knowing AI data-handling and disclosure rules belongs in ai-literacy. Writing a team's AI-use policy belongs in quality-frameworks.
cards.distinctions: Unlike contracts-ip-licensing and ai-literacy, which are knowledge of rules, this bundle is the habit of acting on them with integrity. Unlike quality-frameworks, it is personal conduct, not a review system.
positiveExamples: Credit collaborators and disclose AI's part in a portfolio piece.
Report one's own mistake on a job promptly and propose a fix.
Keep a sponsor's confidential materials out of public work.
negativeExamples: Review a font license before a job's release (belongs in contracts-ip-licensing)
Explain how a generative AI tool can produce wrong output (belongs in ai-literacy)
Write the studio's policy on disclosing AI-generated content (belongs in quality-frameworks)

cards.name: Project management across creative and production work
cards.includes: This bundle covers managing the plan for a creative, print, or packaging project from brief through delivery and close-out: scope, work breakdown, dependencies, critical path, production lead times, schedule, budget, and risk, at different levels of complexity. When a change is requested, it works out the effect on dates and cost, re-baselines the plan, and records the change. It covers spotting early warnings of compounding delays, reporting status and risk to the internal team, and recording lessons learned. Its question is whether the team can deliver and what it will cost.
cards.excludes: Getting the client's sign-offs, explaining a change's trade-offs so the client can decide, and setting client expectations belong in project-oversight; a change request is brought in and decided there, and its impact is planned here. Detailed production cost estimation and equipment payback analysis belong in cost-management. Designing or re-engineering production processes belongs in workflow-design.
cards.distinctions: Unlike project-oversight, which manages the client's decisions, this bundle manages the plan: it owns scope, schedule, budget, dependencies, and risk, and turns an approved change into a re-baselined plan. Unlike cost-management, it integrates the budget with scope, dependencies, schedule, risk, and changes rather than centering on detailed production estimates or equipment justification. Unlike workflow-design, it manages a specific project's life cycle rather than designing or re-engineering the production process.
positiveExamples: Build a packaging project's scope, work breakdown, schedule, and budget across teams and vendors, accounting for dependencies and production lead times.
Work out how a requested change affects the critical path and budget, re-baseline the plan, and record the change.
Report schedule and risk status to the internal team, and document lessons learned at close-out.
negativeExamples: Explain a requested change's timeline and cost trade-offs to the client and get their decision (belongs in project-oversight)
Build a production estimate based on specifications, vendor capability, and run-length economics (belongs in cost-management)
Re-engineer a finishing sequence and validate its effect on throughput and quality (belongs in workflow-design)

cards.name: Client-facing project coordination
cards.includes: This bundle covers managing the client's decisions on a print, packaging, or brand project from brief through delivery. It includes getting sign-off at the handoffs that need it, such as proofs before production; explaining a change's timeline, quality, and cost trade-offs so the client can decide; setting and keeping client expectations; and carrying the client's decision back to the creative and production teams. When a change is requested, it brings the request in and gets the client's decision; the effect on the plan is worked out in project-management. Its question is whether the client knows what they are getting and has agreed.
cards.excludes: Building the schedule and budget, working out a change's impact, and re-baselining the plan belong in project-management; estimating costs and managing spend belongs in cost-management. Configuring an approval or proofing workflow belongs in workflow-architecture, and resolving service problems and keeping the account belong in customer-relationship-management.
cards.distinctions: Unlike project-management, which manages the plan and the change's impact on it, project-oversight manages the client's decisions: sign-offs, expectations, and the client's choice on a change. Unlike customer-relationship-management, its focus is approvals and expectations on a live project rather than resolving service problems and maintaining the account relationship. Unlike team-coordination, it handles client-facing decisions rather than managing staff performance or HR responsibilities.
positiveExamples: Get the client's sign-off on a packaging proof before the handoff to production.
Explain the timeline, quality, and cost trade-offs of a requested change so the client can decide.
Carry an approved client revision back to the creative and prepress teams so everyone works toward the same expectations.
negativeExamples: Work out a change's effect on the critical path and re-baseline the schedule (belongs in project-management)
Configure proof routing and approval steps in a workflow platform (belongs in workflow-architecture)
Resolve a client quality complaint and maintain a relationship record for future account service (belongs in customer-relationship-management)

cards.name: Proposal development, consultative communication, and the ROI case
cards.includes: This bundle covers structuring, writing, and presenting client proposals for print, packaging, brand, or production solutions, using consultative communication to secure commitment and set accurate delivery expectations. It includes justifying scope, sequence, and cost in business terms and building a quantified cost/benefit, ROI, or total cost of ownership case using measures such as payback and cost per unit. The proposal explains why the purchase pays for itself rather than relying on creative appeal or the client relationship alone.
cards.excludes: Discovery conversations that produce a needs assessment belong in client-needs-diagnosis; production cost estimating, spend management, and capital-equipment justification belong in cost-management. Bargaining over price, scope, or terms belongs in negotiation-persuasion, while ongoing client approvals and expectation management during delivery belong in project-oversight. General presentation and speaking skill belongs in spoken-communication.
cards.distinctions: Unlike client-needs-diagnosis, which surfaces the underlying business problem, proposal-development turns a proposed solution into a client-facing case for commitment. Unlike cost-management, which develops production estimates, manages spend, or justifies equipment, this bundle uses costs and benefits to justify the client's purchase in a proposal. Unlike negotiation-persuasion, it centers on explaining and presenting the proposed scope, sequence, cost, and business return rather than bargaining over price, scope, or terms.
positiveExamples: Write a packaging proposal that explains scope, delivery sequence, cost, and quantified client benefits.
Calculate payback and total cost of ownership for a proposed client solution and incorporate them into the purchase case.
Present a print solution proposal, explain its cost-per-unit benefits, and secure client commitment with accurate delivery expectations.
negativeExamples: Conduct a discovery conversation and write an assessment of unstated packaging client needs (belongs in client-needs-diagnosis)
Build a multi-year payback case for a production company's equipment purchase (belongs in cost-management)
Negotiate a print project's price and scope against a defined walk-away point (belongs in negotiation-persuasion)

cards.name: Quality control systems and standards enforcement
cards.includes: This bundle covers setting up and operating the system that catches defects while a print or packaging job is produced and decides whether it ships. It includes setting tolerances, placing inspection points at production handoffs so problems are caught before final inspection, statistical process control of a running process, and accept/reject decisions. Color is one of many things it watches, alongside registration, trapping, dimensions, die lines, barcode grades, and substrate defects. It includes working to production practice standards such as FTA FIRST and using measurement instruments to check conformance.
cards.excludes: Calibration, ICC profiling, and setting up a process to reproduce a color target (G7, ISO 12647) belong in color-management. Interpreting brand rules for a creative deliverable belongs in brand-standards-application. Managing packaging artwork versions and regulatory compliance checks belongs in packaging-artwork-compliance, while configuring workflow platforms for intake, approvals, and reporting belongs in workflow-architecture.
cards.distinctions: Unlike color-management, which sets up color reproduction before the run, quality-control monitors the running job for every kind of defect, color included, and decides whether output is accepted. Unlike quality-frameworks, which covers brand, legal/regulatory, and AI-assisted review steps in a workflow, this bundle centers on production defects and measured conformance. Unlike workflow-design, which designs or re-engineers production processes to balance quality, throughput, and cost, this bundle establishes and operates the checks that enforce quality within those processes.
positiveExamples: Set tolerances and inspection points at production handoffs to catch recurring defects before final inspection.
Use control charts on a running press to spot a drifting process and act before output goes out of tolerance.
Inspect a packaging run for registration, die-line, and barcode-grade defects and decide whether it ships.
negativeExamples: Calibrate and profile a print device to meet a defined color target (belongs in color-management)
Manage packaging artwork versions and check required labeling before release (belongs in packaging-artwork-compliance)
Re-engineer a production step to improve throughput and validate the change (belongs in workflow-design)

cards.name: AI and quality governance
cards.includes: This bundle covers building or operating a brand, legal/regulatory, or print-quality review step in a creative or production workflow that consistently catches failure modes, including those in AI-assisted output. It includes knowing the relevant evaluation standards and where each check belongs in print, packaging, or brand work, and writing or applying an AI-use policy for a team or job: which data may enter which tools, how AI-generated content is disclosed or labeled (including content credentials), and who signs off. It also covers recognizing which checks require domain expertise rather than full automation and keeping a person accountable for AI-assisted output.
cards.excludes: Instrument-based production defect checks belong in quality-control, and color calibration and profiling belong in color-management, and packaging artwork management and versioning belong in packaging-artwork-compliance. Benchmarking AI tools for deployment decisions belongs in ai-tool-evaluation, an individual's knowledge of AI data and disclosure rules belongs in ai-literacy, and setting the organization's AI direction belongs in ai-strategy-change-leadership, while resolving asset licensing and contract risks belongs in contracts-ip-licensing.
cards.distinctions: Unlike quality-control, which emphasizes production quality systems and measured conformance, this bundle emphasizes where quality and compliance reviews belong and the domain judgment and accountability needed to operate them. Unlike packaging-artwork-compliance, it is not centered on managing and versioning packaging artwork files. Unlike ai-tool-evaluation, it checks deliverables within a workflow rather than benchmarking an AI tool to support an adopt, adjust, or drop decision.
positiveExamples: Build a brand review step that consistently catches off-brand elements in creative deliverables, including AI-generated images or copy.
Operate a legal/regulatory review step for print materials, using domain expertise to check issues automated review may miss.
Write a studio's AI-use policy covering what client data may enter which tools, how AI-generated images are disclosed, and who signs off.
negativeExamples: Inspect a press run against production tolerances and decide whether it ships (belongs in quality-control)
Manage packaging artwork versions through a defined regulatory review checklist (belongs in packaging-artwork-compliance)
Benchmark an AI tool against the current process and recommend whether to adopt it (belongs in ai-tool-evaluation)

cards.name: Quantitative literacy
cards.includes: This bundle covers using basic statistical concepts to read research outputs critically in print, packaging, brand, and production work. It includes interpreting data, distinguishing meaningful patterns from noise, and recognizing that a statistically significant difference may not matter in practice. It translates those judgments into recommendations supported by the findings.
cards.excludes: Designing and executing consumer studies belongs in consumer-research; designing measurement frameworks tied to campaign objectives belongs in campaign-measurement. Producing client-facing post-project reports that justify continued investment belongs in results-interpretation.
cards.distinctions: Unlike consumer-research, this bundle focuses on critically interpreting research outputs rather than designing and executing a study. Unlike campaign-measurement, it judges the statistical evidence in results rather than designing a campaign measurement framework. Unlike results-interpretation, it focuses on signal, noise, and practical significance rather than framing a post-project report for client investment decisions.
positiveExamples: Interpret packaging preference research to distinguish a supported pattern from noise.
Explain why a statistically significant difference between print test results may have little practical importance.
Critically read a brand research report and recommend an action supported by its quantitative findings.
negativeExamples: Design and conduct a consumer study comparing packaging concepts (belongs in consumer-research)
Choose campaign measures and connect them to business objectives (belongs in campaign-measurement)
Produce a post-project client report that supports continued investment (belongs in results-interpretation)

cards.name: Resilience
cards.includes: This bundle covers the habit of working through setbacks: failed attempts, critique and open-ended constraints. It is shown by revising after failure and persisting through real difficulty rather than abandoning the work or settling for less, in courses that create genuine setbacks to work through.
cards.excludes: Recovering a client relationship after a service failure belongs in customer-relationship-management. Choosing one's own direction belongs in agency.
cards.distinctions: Unlike agency, which is initiative in making choices, resilience is persistence after things go wrong. Unlike customer-relationship-management, it concerns one's own response to setbacks, not repairing a client's trust.
positiveExamples: Rework a press setup after a failed run and reach an acceptable result.
Revise a design through several rounds of critique without abandoning the concept's strengths.
Keep a project moving after a key approach fails, finding another way to meet the brief.
negativeExamples: Manage a client's complaint about a missed delivery to resolution (belongs in customer-relationship-management)
Choose a project direction from an open brief (belongs in agency)
Investigate why a printing defect occurs beyond what the lab required (belongs in curiosity)

cards.name: Results interpretation and client reporting
cards.includes: This bundle covers interpreting completed brand, print, packaging, or production project results using metrics that matter to the client. It frames those results in terms of business outcomes rather than counts of assets produced or deliverables completed. It includes producing a post-project report the client can use to justify continued investment.
cards.excludes: Designing a campaign measurement framework belongs in campaign-measurement; building a prospective ROI or cost/benefit case for a client proposal belongs in proposal-development. Reading job-costing or profit-and-loss reports to decide whether an account is worth keeping belongs in business-financial-literacy.
cards.distinctions: Unlike campaign-measurement, which designs measurement frameworks and evaluates campaign effectiveness, results-interpretation focuses on explaining completed-project results in a client-facing report. Unlike proposal-development, it uses results already achieved rather than a proposed solution's projected benefits to support investment. Unlike business-financial-literacy, it explains value to the client rather than judging whether a job or account is profitable for the provider.
positiveExamples: Identify which completed-project metrics matter to a brand or production client's investment decision.
Explain what reported project results mean for the client's business outcomes rather than listing deliverable counts.
Produce a post-project report that supports the client's justification for continued investment.
negativeExamples: Design a campaign measurement framework tied to business objectives (belongs in campaign-measurement)
Build a quantified ROI case for a proposed print solution (belongs in proposal-development)
Use a job-costing report to determine whether an account is profitable to retain (belongs in business-financial-literacy)

cards.name: Spoken communication
cards.includes: This bundle covers presenting, explaining and listening well in speech: presentations, critiques, and client and team conversations, adjusted to the audience, with questions handled well. It is shown through graded presentations, critiques and spoken exchanges whose rubric assesses the communication itself.
cards.excludes: Writing belongs in written-communication. Persuading in a negotiation belongs in negotiation-persuasion, and consultative selling of a solution belongs in proposal-development. Getting a client's decision on a live project belongs in project-oversight.
cards.distinctions: Unlike written-communication, it is communication in speech. Unlike negotiation-persuasion and proposal-development, which are business skills that use speaking, this bundle is the general ability to speak and listen well.
positiveExamples: Present a design solution to a class critique and respond to questions clearly.
Explain a technical production issue to a non-technical audience.
Listen to a client's concerns in a meeting and restate them accurately before responding.
negativeExamples: Write a specification a printer can quote from (belongs in written-communication)
Negotiate a job price against a walk-away point (belongs in negotiation-persuasion)
Get a client's sign-off on a proof before production (belongs in project-oversight)

cards.name: Systems automation and integration
cards.includes: This bundle covers using scripts, APIs, or low-code automation tools to connect creative, production workflow, and AI systems in print, packaging, or brand work. It includes understanding the data each system sends and expects, where the connection can break, and how to handle those failures rather than only a successful transfer. The practical work is building or configuring an automation for a real handoff between two systems that includes a generative-AI step.
cards.excludes: Designing intake, approval, proofing, and reporting sequences belongs in workflow-architecture; directing prompts and iterating AI output for brand quality belongs in ai-tool-direction. Benchmarking an AI tool's quality, cost, and consistency to recommend adoption belongs in ai-tool-evaluation.
cards.distinctions: Unlike workflow-architecture, which defines and sequences workflow steps, this bundle implements the automated connection between systems. Unlike ai-tool-direction, which centers on directing AI output and building personal tools, it centers on a real cross-system handoff and both systems' data and failure modes. Unlike ai-tool-evaluation, it focuses on making the integration work rather than benchmarking an AI step to support an adoption decision.
positiveExamples: Configure a low-code handoff from a creative intake system to a generative-AI service, mapping input fields and handling missing data.
Write an API integration that transfers AI-generated copy into a packaging artwork workflow and handles failed responses.
Test a scripted handoff between a creative system and an AI system with incompatible data and unavailable-service cases.
negativeExamples: Configure the sequence of intake, human approval, and AI work in a creative workflow platform (belongs in workflow-architecture)
